title: Help make back to school season safe in Kitchener
content: On September 8, schools across Kitchener will welcome new and returning students to their classrooms. With increased traffic during drop-off and pick-up times, we ask that you leave extra time when travelling and stay aware to help make this a safe back to school season for all.

The new Notre Dame Catholic Secondary School at 20 Woolner Trail is open for the 2026/27 school year, which means there are new road rules in and around the school zone. Pay attention to and comply with new speed limits, no stopping zones and school bus loading zones in this neighbourhood. Bylaw enforcement will be in effect.

There is a new crossing guard location at Fairway Road and Woolner Trail in addition to established crossing guard locations across the city. Visit the pedestrians and sidewalks webpage for a full list of crossing guard times and locations.

title: More vendors return to Kitchener Market this Saturday
content: Kitchener, ON – Residents will have even more opportunities to shop local this Saturday as additional vendors return to the Kitchener Market, marking another milestone in the Market's recovery. Visitors can expect an expanded lineup of farmers, food producers and local businesses while restoration work continues inside the Market building.

The Kitchener Market has remained open every Saturday since the July fire, providing customers with access to local food and products while vendors continue serving the community. Investments in temporary electrical, plumbing and water infrastructure have expanded operations into the breezeway and parking lot of the building, making it possible for more vendors to return quickly and safely. This investment in temporary infrastructure is creating additional shopping options for residents and supporting business continuity while restoration work continues. The City is proactively preparing the space for colder weather to support continued market operations through the fall and winter months, so vendors can continue serving customers comfortably while restoration work continues.

"The resilience shown by our vendors throughout this recovery has been remarkable," said Councillor Stephanie Stretch. "Despite challenging circumstances, vendors have continued to adapt, serve customers and support one another. Their resilience is a testament to the strength of the Market community. Now more than ever, choosing to shop locally makes a meaningful difference for the small businesses that help make Kitchener the vibrant city that it is."

For more than 155 years, the Market has connected residents with local farmers, entrepreneurs and food producers. Every purchase made at the Market helps support local jobs, local families and the local economy. The Kitchener Market remains a vital community hub where residents can connect directly with the people who grow, raise, bake and make products close to home.

Restoration work is underway and the City remains focused on maintaining market operations while working toward welcoming vendors and visitors back inside the Market building as soon as it is safe to do so.

title: Storm Cleanup Response - September 3
content: A severe storm moved through Kitchener on  Wednesday, September 2, 2026. Strong winds caused extensive damage to trees in many areas of the city.
The City prioritized clearing roadways first, then driveways, followed by sidewalks. City crews will continue working across Kitchener to clear and clean up debris on public property.
Public safety

While the most urgent needs and issues have been addressed, we continue to remind members of the public to be aware of the damage that may remain in upright trees and are at risk of falling. Please do not climb downed trees or around upturned root balls, respect work areas around forestry crews and obey signs, barriers, and fences around areas that are closed.
Responding to downed power lines
If residents see downed power lines, they should stay 10-metres away from the downed line, call 9-1-1- and report it to Enova Power by calling 226-896-2200.
Downed power lines may still be energized and deadly, and the ground around the line could be live, even if it looks dry or safe (Enova Power).
Responding to fallen branches/trees
If a City-owned tree on the boulevard in front of a resident’s home has fallen or been damaged during the storm, it can be reported to the City’s Corporate Contact Centre at 519-741-2345.

Residents are responsible for the cleanup of trees on their private property. The City will clean up city-owned trees that have fallen onto private property, but we will not clean up private trees. If a private tree is blocking the roadway or impacting public property, we will assist in making it safe, but the remaining cleanup is the responsibility of private property owners.
Residents are encouraged to take debris directly to the  Waste Management Site for disposal.
Residents are being asked to manage debris on their properties and can dispose of fallen trees or branches by trimming them into manageable pieces
Bundle branches securely and place them out with their curbside yard waste. For tips on how to properly prepare yard waste for curbside collection, visit Yard Waste | Region of Waterloo
Compost them in backyard compost
Fallen trees or branches should not be disposed of in City parks, forests or trails.
Staying prepared

Staying up to date on current and forecast weather conditions is one of the best ways to prepare for severe weather. Check local weather stations regularly for weather watches and warnings and sign up for local emergency alerts through Alert Waterloo Region .

To prepare for severe weather, make a family emergency plan and have practice drills so everyone knows what to do; develop a protocol for staying in contact with family and friends, like a group chat, social media group or list of contact details; and build a 72-hour emergency kit that allows your family to be self-sustaining for at least three days. More information on preparing for an emergency is available on the Province of Ontario’s website .

title: Welcoming Week celebration connects newcomers with community resources and supports
content: Whether you're new to Kitchener or planning to make the city your home, finding the right information and community connections can make all the difference.

As part of Welcoming Week , the City of Kitchener is inviting residents to join our Welcoming Week Kitchener event on Saturday, September 12 . This free community celebration brings people together to connect with neighbours, discover local programs and services, and learn about the many resources available to help newcomers feel at home in Kitchener.
Connect with local organizations and City services

Event details

Attendees will have the opportunity to connect directly with City services staff, organizations that provide newcomer services, settlement supports, employment resources, language assistance, recreation opportunities and community programs.
The event will also feature:
No registration is required. Everyone is welcome.

title: Severe weather impacts - September 2 - 9:30 pm
content: Updated at 9:30 p.m.

As of 9:30 p.m., Kitchener forestry crews have received more than 60 calls regarding downed trees and debris. Crews are working late this evening to address issues, prioritizing clearing roadways, then driveways, then sidewalks, and will return to non-urgent areas in the morning. There may be an impact to residents' morning commute.

Otherwise, we expect a return to normal operations for most City programs and services tomorrow, but continue to check Kitchener.ca/news for the latest updates. We appreciate residents' patience as crews work to respond to priority areas and clear debris safely.
Environment and Climate Change Canada has issued a severe thunderstorm watch for Waterloo Region, with a severe weather threat expected to develop this afternoon.
This includes conditions favourable to produce tornados along a line running from Grand Bend through London and into the Kitchener area.  Other potential severe impacts could include:
Damaging wind gusts (up to 130 km/h)
Heavy short-duration rainfall or downpours (up to 50 mm)
Large hail up to 5 cm (golf ball)
Please take cover immediately if threatening weather approaches.

title: City of Kitchener celebrates Culture Days with two weeks of free arts and culture experiences
content: The City of Kitchener is inviting residents and visitors to explore, create and connect through two weeks of concerts, performances, art demonstrations and hands-on activities during Culture Days 2026. This province-wide celebration of arts, culture and heritage is  running from September 18 to October 4, wrapping up a summer of events that has celebrated arts and entertainment through the launch of Kitchener LIVE and welcomed over 100,000 residents and visitors to a season of celebration. Throughout the festival, Kitchener will be home to dozens of free experiences led by the City and local arts and cultural organizations, showcasing the creativity and talent that make the community unique.

“Kitchener’s investments in arts and culture helps build a vibrant, welcoming community where people can connect, share experiences, and celebrate the diversity that makes Kitchener special, and builds a sense of belonging amongst residents and visitors alike,” said Mayor Berry Vrbanovic. “Culture Days is an opportunity to experience the creativity that exists in every corner of our city while supporting the Canadian artists, organizations and cultural leaders who enrich community life year-round.”

The festival features a wide range of activities offered by local arts and cultural organizations, including artist talks and walks, exhibitions, workshops, heritage experiences, public art events, live music and more.

As part of the celebration, the City of Kitchener will host a special weekend of programming from September 25 to 27, featuring live music, visual arts and opportunities to connect directly with local artists. Highlights include:

Friday, September 25 – A Culture Days kickoff at Kitchener City Hall featuring a free concert with country music performers Amanda & James and Chris Clark, along with artist talks from two local artists to open their exhibits in the Berlin Tower ARTSPACE and Rotunda Gallery.

Saturday, September 26 –  A series of pop-up performances across downtown, including a Beatles-inspired rooftop concert at the The Yeti and opera performances at Kitchener City Hall. Visitors can also enjoy the Gaukel Block Arts Festival, featuring live mural painting and music featuring Evan Redsky and Mandippal.
Sunday, September 27 – An open house and block party at 44 Gaukel, where visitors can tour artist studios, meet local creatives and take part in interactive arts experiences.

Throughout the two-week celebration, there are even more art demonstrations, performances and activities hosted by local arts organizations throughout the city, with something happening every day from September 18 to October 4.

“Culture Days gives artists the opportunity to share their work, spark imagination and invite people into the creative process,” said Andrea Hallam, Manager of Arts and Creative Industries for the City of Kitchener. “Whether you're discovering a new musician, meeting a visual artist in their studio or trying a hands-on creative activity, these experiences help people see the world in new ways and deepen appreciation for the arts in our community.”
Whether you're an art lover, music fan or simply curious, Culture Days offers countless ways to experience the creativity that brings Kitchener to life.
Explore everything Culture Days has in store at KitchenerLive.ca/CultureDays

title: Statement by Kitchener Mayor Berry Vrbanovic on the Canada-U.S. Trade Conflict
content: Yesterday evening, during the regularly scheduled City Council meeting, Kitchener Mayor Berry Vrbanovic provided the following statement on the current Canada-US Trade Conflict:
Colleagues,

On Friday evening, just past midnight, Canadians learned that there was a breakdown in negotiations between our Canadian government with the current US Administration in the White House pertaining to the threat of tariffs previously announced by the US President.  As such Prime Minister Carney called back Canada’s negotiating team to Ottawa and communicated news of this to Canadians on Friday evening via a media statement and via a Press Conference on Saturday morning.  These were followed by a meeting with the Premiers and the Cabinet.

Since news of this first broke, Canada’s Premiers, national business organizations and leaders have rallied around the Prime Minister and our government. I would frame the messages heard over the last 72 plus hours around three main themes: 1. Canadian unity around protecting Canadian sovereignty, 2. protecting local jobs and businesses, and 3. using this moment to accelerate economic resilience and diversification.
Sadly, our long-time neighbour, partner and ally made the choices they did in negotiations, but our Canadian negotiators stood firm and recognized that no deal is better than a bad deal.

Over the course of the weekend, I have been in touch with various provincial and federal officials, and also offered an initial statement via social media, thanking them all for their tireless efforts over many months, and especially in recent weeks on behalf of Canadians and I also extended our gratitude to them for standing together as one team, united for Canada.

The breakdown of Canada–U.S. trade negotiations and the imposition of the new tariffs mark a deeply concerning escalation in an economic conflict that neither country ultimately wins. As Canadians, I believe we must stay united: Canada must remain open to negotiations, but we cannot accept a deal that compromises our economic interests or sovereignty or we cannot go back to the table if there isn’t a meaningful rationale provided by our US partners in this regard.

For Kitchener, this is particularly challenging. Our local manufacturing economy is deeply connected to continental supply chains, and export markets. When tariffs disrupt those relationships, the consequences are felt by local employers, workers and families.
That is why this evening I am sharing that earlier today I have asked staff to resume the City of Kitchener’s Tariff and Trade Task Force that was originally started in 2025.

When this challenge first emerged at that time, our Task Force moved quickly. We strengthened Buy Canadian and Buy Local procurement, worked with suppliers to identify Canadian alternatives, engaged directly with trade-exposed businesses, supported import substitution, and launched our Support Local campaign with community and business partners.
Now we must go further.

I will ask the Task Force to examine additional opportunities to strengthen local and Canadian procurement; support affected businesses and workers; identify our most vulnerable industries for government advocacy; help companies diversify into new Canadian and international markets; and work with other governments and business organizations, including BestWR to advocate for meaningful assistance.

Kitchener has always been a community of makers, innovators and entrepreneurs. In this moment of uncertainty, it’s important that we all stand together — supporting local, buying Canadian, protecting jobs and building a stronger, more resilient economy for a stronger Kitchener and Waterloo region, a stronger Ontario and a stronger Canada.

title: Music to connect generations: Amanda Braam named Kitchener’s 2026 Artist in Residence
content: The City of Kitchener is pleased to announce Amanda Braam as the City’s 2026 Artist in Residence. Braam, a Kitchener-based singer-songwriter, musician and recent graduate of Wilfrid Laurier University's music therapy program, will lead the City’s first Musician in Residence program since 2019 with a project that will bring generations together through music.

“Congratulations to Amanda on being selected as Kitchener’s next Artist in Residence,” said Mayor Berry Vrbanovic. “Amanda’s project embodies the spirit of connection, creativity and community that makes Kitchener such a vibrant place to live. As we continue building on the momentum of Kitchener Live, our new live entertainment platform launched earlier this year, this residency will help strengthen our growing music ecosystem, create meaningful opportunities for residents to engage with local music, and support the next generation of artists and music leaders in our city.”

Kitchener’s Artist in Residence program supports artistic innovation while creating opportunities for artists to engage and collaborate with the community. For 2026, the residency was designed to support musicians, music educators and music entrepreneurs in creating meaningful, community-engaged musical experiences for residents of all ages.

During her residency, Braam will develop a community-focused music project aimed at bridging generations through music, creating opportunities for residents of different ages to connect, collaborate and share experiences through musical participation.

“We received many thoughtful and inspiring proposals, which speaks to the incredible depth of musical talent in our community,” said William Muir, the City of Kitchener's Music Officer. “Supporting emerging local artists is essential to a healthy and sustainable music sector. Amanda’s residency will create opportunities for learning, mentorship and collaboration while enriching the experiences of musicians and residents alike. We’re excited to see the connections and creativity that will emerge through this project.”

Braam will begin her residency in September 2026 and work with community partners, local musicians and residents throughout the year to bring her project to life. The residency is intended to support artistic development while fostering meaningful relationships between artists and the community.
For more information about Kitchener’s Artist in Residence program, visit Kitchener.ca/AIR
